body.Emerging Risk: AI governance, integrity, and accountability in high-consequence workflows
body.SET Risk Owner: IT; Digital; R&D; Regulatory; Quality; Legal; Medical; Clinical
body.Risk Statement: AZ may increasingly rely on AI-supported outputs in regulated scientific, medical, quality, operational, commercial, and clinical-development workflows without sufficiently mature standards for validation, provenance, accountability, review, and control of derived or unstructured data.
body.Why Emerging Now: AI use is expanding from productivity into evidence generation, clinical-development support, content, and high-consequence operational or scientific decision support faster than internal and external assurance models are maturing.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could affect the defensibility, safety, and reliability of decisions across R&D, medical, quality, supply, clinical development, and commercial execution, with compliance, trust, and value-realization implications.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: AI-supported outputs materially influencing high-consequence decisions without clear accountability or defensible review; repeated questions on traceability, validation, explainability, or underlying data quality; governance exceptions becoming normalized.
body.ER_Cluster: Automation, AI, and trusted data at scale

body.Emerging Risk: Opaque or weakly provable AI and data-derived evidence chains
body.SET Risk Owner: R&D; Regulatory; Quality; IT; Medical; Legal; Clinical
body.Risk Statement: AZ may become dependent on high-performing but insufficiently explainable or reproducible AI and data systems in discovery, development, medical, and operational settings, making evidence chains harder to defend and investigate.
body.Why Emerging Now: Model performance is improving across multimodal, scientific, clinical, and operational use cases even where explainability, reproducibility, and investigability lag.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could weaken the ability to defend major scientific, operational, clinical, or medical decisions, making failures harder to investigate and external confidence harder to sustain.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Material decisions rely on AI or complex data systems that cannot be satisfactorily reproduced, challenged, or investigated; repeated disputes over explainability or defensibility.
body.ER_Cluster: Automation, AI, and trusted data at scale

body.Emerging Risk: Training-data rights, proprietary knowledge exposure, and model provenance uncertainty
body.SET Risk Owner: Legal; IP; Procurement; IT; R&D; Commercial
body.Risk Statement: Uncertainty over training-data rights, output ownership, vendor use of data, derived-data obligations, third-party AI contracting, and contamination of proprietary scientific, clinical, or commercial know-how may constrain AZ’s ability to scale AI confidently.
body.Why Emerging Now: Commercial norms, legal interpretations, and technical controls remain uneven while AI adoption is accelerating across data-rich enterprise environments and third-party AI arrangements.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could expose AZ to disputes over ownership, restrict use of AI-enabled outputs, weaken defensibility of models and content, and create loss of competitive edge through poorly governed data, model, or third-party arrangements.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Evidence of unclear ownership or use rights in data or model arrangements; inability to evidence provenance for critical outputs; contractual terms proving insufficient for strategic AI use; shadow AI or third-party arrangements bypassing expected controls.
body.ER_Cluster: Automation, AI, and trusted data at scale

body.Emerging Risk: Fragmented and tightening AI control regimes across health, workplace, and operations
body.SET Risk Owner: Legal; Compliance; IT; Regulatory; HR; Quality; Manufacturing
body.Risk Statement: AZ may face increasingly fragmented and formalized AI rules affecting health, workplace, operational, content, and decision-support use cases across multiple regions.
body.Why Emerging Now: Authorities are moving from broad AI principles toward more specific obligations on logging, oversight, certification, transparency, workplace use, and local control.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could force region-specific deployment models, increase compliance burden, delay scaling of AI-enabled processes, and fragment enterprise operating approaches.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: New AI rules materially constrain deployment, require redesign, or create conflicting obligations across jurisdictions; local AI governance becomes a barrier to scale.
body.ER_Cluster: Automation, AI, and trusted data at scale

body.Emerging Risk: Trust and disclosure challenges in AI-enabled medical, scientific, and commercial content
body.SET Risk Owner: Medical; Corporate Affairs; Commercial; Legal; Compliance; Digital
body.Risk Statement: Stakeholders may challenge AZ’s use of AI in scientific communication, medical content, commercial materials, or external engagement if disclosure, authorship, and quality expectations are not clear or aligned.
body.Why Emerging Now: AI is moving visibly into content creation and external-facing workflows at a time of heightened sensitivity to authenticity, transparency, and misinformation.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could undermine trust, create reputational spillover, and increase challenge from regulators, clinicians, patients, or policymakers regarding the integrity of AZ communications.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Controversy over undisclosed or poorly governed use of AI in external content; criticism of content accuracy, authenticity, or transparency linked to AI use.
body.ER_Cluster: Automation, AI, and trusted data at scale

body.Emerging Risk: Product liability expansion across AI-enabled decision chains
body.SET Risk Owner: Legal; Compliance; IT; Medical; Quality; Risk
body.Risk Statement: Liability may expand where outcomes reflect combinations of humans, AI systems, external data, software, and third-party platforms across medical, operational, clinical-support, and support decisions.
body.Why Emerging Now: Legal regimes are evolving toward stricter and more claimant-friendly approaches to software, AI, and complex chains of responsibility, including expanded supply-chain liability concepts.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could increase litigation exposure, contractual complexity, insurance challenge, and evidentiary burden where AI or software materially shapes decisions, recommendations, or product-related outcomes.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Court decisions, directives, or enforcement materially increase liability exposure for AI-influenced or software-dependent processes; contracts fail to allocate responsibility credibly.
body.ER_Cluster: Automation, AI, and trusted data at scale

body.Emerging Risk: Global governance regimes for autonomous scientific and medical systems
body.SET Risk Owner: Legal; Regulatory; R&D; IT; Medical
body.Risk Statement: Authorities may move beyond regulating outputs to regulating autonomous scientific, medical, or operational AI systems themselves through licensing, inspection, or operating standards.
body.Why Emerging Now: AI may increasingly act in scientific, clinical-support, and operational environments in ways that challenge existing concepts of oversight and machine responsibility.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could impose new licensing, inspection, and operating obligations on autonomous research or medical systems, increasing compliance burden and limiting flexibility.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Formal governance initiatives target autonomous scientific or medical AI systems rather than only specific uses or outputs.
body.ER_Cluster: Automation, AI, and trusted data at scale

body.Emerging Risk: Post-human comparative decision environments in pharma and healthcare
body.SET Risk Owner: Strategy; Risk; HR; Regulatory; IT
body.Risk Statement: AI may outperform humans across broad clusters of analytical, coordination, and optimization tasks relevant to AZ’s science, operations, and healthcare-facing activities.
body.Why Emerging Now: Long-run AI trajectories point toward wider machine superiority in knowledge-intensive and system-level tasks rather than isolated productivity use cases.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could fundamentally reshape the role of human expertise, escalation, and authority across AZ’s operating model and external healthcare interfaces.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: AI becomes demonstrably superior across multiple decision domains relevant to AZ, creating pressure to redesign governance and human roles.
body.ER_Cluster: Automation, AI, and trusted data at scale

body.Emerging Risk: Concentration risk in cloud, model, software, and platform ecosystems
body.SET Risk Owner: IT; Cyber; Procurement; Enterprise Risk; Digital
body.Risk Statement: AZ may become strategically overdependent on a small number of cloud, model, software, and platform providers that underpin scientific, commercial, clinical, and operational workflows, including shared AI stacks whose common-mode failure or strategic restriction could disrupt multiple critical processes at once.
body.Why Emerging Now: Digital backbone concentration is increasing while more critical processes rely on third-party platforms, software dependencies, and shared model ecosystems, increasing the chance that failures are correlated rather than isolated and that access may be restricted or used as a source of geopolitical or commercial leverage.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could interrupt critical workflows, increase cost, weaken negotiating leverage, reduce resilience, and expose AZ to geopolitical or commercial leverage if major providers change terms, fail, or experience common-mode disruption across shared AI or software dependencies.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Material business workflows depend on a small number of external providers; outages, model withdrawal, or term changes significantly disrupt activity; fallback options prove inadequate; or a shared AI/software dependency causes simultaneous disruption across multiple functions.

body.Emerging Risk: Distributed operational compute and edge-AI control complexity
body.SET Risk Owner: IT; Cyber; Quality; Operations; Manufacturing
body.Risk Statement: As AZ deploys more local inference, edge AI, and distributed compute in sites, labs, devices, and partner settings, control environments may fragment faster than assurance and support models, especially where hidden software dependencies and locally varied configurations create correlated control fragility.
body.Why Emerging Now: Operational AI is increasingly shaped by distributed compute, latency-sensitive use cases, local hosting expectations, and heterogeneous software environments rather than only centralized cloud, making hidden single points of failure harder to see and manage.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could create inconsistent validated states, patching and auditability problems, resilience gaps, and higher exposure in site-level or device-level AI-enabled operations.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Edge or local inference becomes business-critical without clear architecture, validation, patching, failover, and support standards.

body.Emerging Risk: Sovereign compute asymmetry and restricted access to strategic digital capability
body.SET Risk Owner: IT; Strategy; Legal; R&D; Finance
body.Risk Statement: Access to frontier compute, semiconductors, AI ecosystems, core software, and secure digital infrastructure may become uneven across regions, affecting where AZ can compete most effectively.
body.Why Emerging Now: Compute and digital capability are becoming strategic assets shaped by industrial policy, export controls, regional preference, sovereign digital strategy, pricing power, and selective access to advanced model or software capability.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could create regional disparities in scientific speed, analytics capability, commercial AI effectiveness, and operating leverage, forcing uneven regional models and exposing AZ to future pricing or access shocks from concentrated providers.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Access to required compute, frontier models, or critical enterprise software becomes materially constrained, selectively restricted, or significantly more expensive in regions important to AZ’s science or operations.

body.Emerging Risk: Data, model, and scientific sovereignty fragmentation
body.SET Risk Owner: IT; Legal; R&D; Clinical; Regulatory
body.Risk Statement: National or regional control over datasets, model weights, patient data, scientific assets, hosting location, and AI methods may hinder AZ’s ability to operate globally integrated science and analytics models.
body.Why Emerging Now: Data localization, AI sovereignty, health-data restrictions, and strategic treatment of scientific assets are expanding across multiple jurisdictions, including more controlled or federated models in Europe and selective ‘trusted company’ access dynamics.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could force duplication of platforms, models, studies, and reporting structures; reduce collaboration efficiency; constrain AI development; and weaken the scale benefits of AZ’s global science model, including areas where AZ currently benefits from access to Chinese science.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Cross-border data or model use becomes materially harder in key markets; regional rules disrupt study design, analytics, model sharing, or enterprise reporting; access depends on local hosting, entity structure, or trusted-status conditions.

body.Emerging Risk: Quantum-era cryptographic exposure in long-lived data and digital infrastructure
body.SET Risk Owner: Cyber; IT; Digital; R&D; Legal
body.Risk Statement: AZ may face exposure if long-lived sensitive data or systems are compromised by future cryptographic breaks before post-quantum transition is complete.
body.Why Emerging Now: Adversaries may already be harvesting encrypted data while post-quantum transition planning remains immature in many sectors.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could expose sensitive scientific, patient, operational, or commercial data and create complex remediation or trust impacts across long-lived digital systems.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Critical data or systems are judged vulnerable to future decryption risk without credible migration plans.

body.Emerging Risk: Specialized manufacturing capacity concentration for advanced modalities and launches
body.SET Risk Owner: Manufacturing; Supply Chain; External Manufacturing; PT&D; Strategy
body.Risk Statement: AZ may face structural fragility if future growth depends on a limited number of specialized internal or external manufacturing nodes for complex modalities and launch-critical products within a more automated, intelligent, and tightly integrated supply model.
body.Why Emerging Now: Advanced modalities, sterile processes, autonomous manufacturing ambitions, and launch-sensitive supply depend on scarce qualified capacity, partners, and technical transfer success.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could delay launches, constrain scale-up, reduce recovery options, and increase dependence on a small number of critical sites or partners.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Portfolio-critical products become dependent on too few qualified sites or partners; capacity or transfer bottlenecks delay launch or remediation.

body.Emerging Risk: Automation-stack and digital-industrial fragility in quality-critical operations
body.SET Risk Owner: Manufacturing; Quality; Engineering; IT; Operations
body.Risk Statement: AZ’s manufacturing and laboratory environments may become more fragile as validated operations depend on robotics, vision systems, digital twins, MES/LIMS integration, and connected industrial platforms.
body.Why Emerging Now: Physical AI, connected operations, and digital-industrial integration are expanding faster than resilient validated architectures are standardizing.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could impair continuity, extend recovery times, increase validation burden, and create hidden single points of failure in high-consequence operational environments.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Critical operations depend on validated automation stacks that prove hard to remediate, replace, or recover after disruption or change.

body.Emerging Risk: Cyber-physical disruption in connected manufacturing and labs
body.SET Risk Owner: Cyber; Manufacturing; Quality; IT; Engineering
body.Risk Statement: Connected OT, lab automation, robotics fleets, environmental controls, and digitally linked operations may create new pathways for silent or high-impact disruption of physical operations.
body.Why Emerging Now: Manufacturing and scientific digitalization are increasing both connectivity and operational attack surface, while cyber incidents increasingly trigger overlapping privacy, product-quality, safety, and critical-infrastructure obligations.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could cause site outages, batch loss, quality failure, delayed release, patient impact, regulatory scrutiny, and costly recovery where digital disruption affects physical operations.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: A cyber or digital integrity event materially affects manufacturing, lab, or quality operations; operational recovery proves more difficult than expected; overlapping cyber/privacy/product obligations are triggered.

body.Emerging Risk: Hidden dependence on scarce specialist operational and validation expertise
body.SET Risk Owner: Manufacturing; Quality; HR; IT; Engineering
body.Risk Statement: Small pools of experts may hold disproportionate tacit knowledge in aseptic quality, validation, automation integration, digital-industrial systems, and remediation of high-consequence operational issues.
body.Why Emerging Now: Hybrid regulated-operations and advanced-automation skills are scarce while complexity and transformation demands are increasing.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could weaken resilience, slow issue resolution and transformation, increase succession risk, and create hidden single points of failure in critical operational processes.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: One or two people or teams become clear single points of failure for quality-critical or automation-critical operations; vacancies remain unfilled for long periods.

body.Emerging Risk: Site viability divergence driven by infrastructure, utilities, resource stress, and regulatory adaptation burden
body.SET Risk Owner: Manufacturing; Engineering; Real Estate; Sustainability; Strategy
body.Risk Statement: Some AZ sites may become structurally less attractive as advanced manufacturing and supply depend more on grid stability, water, wastewater, transport, connectivity, climate resilience, and the ability to adapt to rising environmental and regulatory expectations.
body.Why Emerging Now: Site resilience increasingly depends on both physical utilities and digital-industrial infrastructure, while climate stress, infrastructure pressure, and local adaptation requirements are increasing.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could raise resilience capex, impair continuity, reduce deployment options for next-generation operations, and alter long-term footprint choices.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Repeated utility, infrastructure, or permitting stress materially affects site economics, continuity, or suitability for strategic investment.

body.Emerging Risk: Distributed, personalized, and care-linked manufacturing control complexity
body.SET Risk Owner: Manufacturing; Quality; Regulatory; Strategy
body.Risk Statement: AZ may need to manage more localized, modular, patient-specific, or care-linked production models that strain current QA, release, accountability, and enterprise-control assumptions.
body.Why Emerging Now: Personalized therapies, modular systems, and distributed manufacturing models are developing alongside more orchestrated automation and digital control.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could increase operational complexity, require redesigned control frameworks, and change the enterprise boundary between AZ, partners, providers, and care settings.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Distributed or care-linked production scales to the point that existing QA, release, and governance models become inadequate.

body.Emerging Risk: Mandatory resilience, localization, and continuity obligations for strategic medicines
body.SET Risk Owner: Supply Chain; Manufacturing; Government Affairs; Finance; Legal
body.Risk Statement: Governments may increasingly require AZ to hold stock, localize capability, increase transparency, dual-source, or meet higher resilience standards for essential or strategic medicines.
body.Why Emerging Now: Medicine shortages, industrial policy, health-security concerns, and the possibility that medicines are treated more like strategic sectors are increasing political pressure for pharmaceutical resilience obligations, supply-chain localization, and biosecurity-oriented operating requirements.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could raise fixed cost, reduce network flexibility, require redesign of supply models, and change the economics of selected products and geographies.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Legislation, procurement rules, or designation of AZ operations as strategically critical materially affect network design or resilience cost.

body.Emerging Risk: Upstream supplier-network opacity and N-tier dependency risk
body.SET Risk Owner: Procurement; Supply Chain; Manufacturing; Legal; Compliance; Enterprise Risk
body.Risk Statement: Limited visibility beyond Tier 1 suppliers may leave AZ unable to detect upstream fragility, contractual exposure, dependency concentration, transport and storage constraints, or emerging regulatory and ESG issues until they disrupt supply, cost, or compliance.
body.Why Emerging Now: AZ’s supply resilience increasingly depends on understanding upstream networks, material dependencies, and real rather than assumed contractual and regulatory positions across complex supplier ecosystems.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could leave material vulnerabilities and contractual exposure unquantified, reduce sourcing agility, delay response to disruption, and create unknown-unknown exposure across critical supply chains.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: AZ cannot quantify exposure across important supplier networks; material disruptions or compliance issues originate upstream without sufficient early warning; N-tier visibility remains incomplete in critical categories.

body.Emerging Risk: Stranded manufacturing and legacy site asset risk
body.SET Risk Owner: Manufacturing; Finance; Engineering; Sustainability; Strategy
body.Risk Statement: Parts of AZ’s manufacturing network may become underutilized, strategically misaligned, or environmentally burdened if therapeutic mix, production models, and regulatory expectations shift faster than the economic life of existing assets.
body.Why Emerging Now: AZ has invested heavily in long-life manufacturing infrastructure while portfolio mix, personalized medicine, production technologies, and environmental expectations may evolve in ways that reduce the relevance of some legacy configurations.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could lead to impairment charges, accelerated depreciation, remediation cost, lower returns on invested capital, and forced reinvestment in more flexible or modality-appropriate capacity.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Sustained underutilization of important assets; material mismatch between network configuration and future pipeline needs; emerging unprovisioned environmental liabilities at older sites.

body.Emerging Risk: Human-to-AI capability crossover in knowledge-intensive work
body.SET Risk Owner: HR; IT; R&D; Regulatory; GFS; Quality
body.Risk Statement: AI may outperform many humans in first-pass drafting, coding, synthesis, analytical, and triage tasks across functions important to AZ.
body.Why Emerging Now: Model capability is improving quickly while enterprise adoption is accelerating across knowledge-heavy work.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could reshape role design, reduce human familiarity with core tasks, alter control models, and create both productivity gains and capability risks.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: A material share of scientific, regulatory, financial, or operational work becomes routinely AI-first, with human roles changing faster than capability and accountability models.

body.Emerging Risk: Erosion of developmental pathways, succession depth, and critical-skills supply
body.SET Risk Owner: HR; Functional Leaders; Manufacturing; Quality; GFS; R&D; Digital
body.Risk Statement: Automation, AI, and changing work design may reduce the developmental pathways, knowledge transfer, succession depth, and critical-skills supply AZ needs across science, operations, digital, finance, regulatory, and commercial functions.
body.Why Emerging Now: AZ is scaling AI, digital, and transformation-led ways of working while many functions face shrinking feeder roles, fewer foundational tasks, and rising dependence on a narrower pool of senior experts to perform, teach, and govern critical work.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could weaken long-term capability formation, reduce succession resilience, increase dependence on a smaller pool of internal or external experts, and create projected capability gaps against Strategy 2030 demand.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Entry-level or developmental roles shrink materially without credible replacement mechanisms for capability building; business-critical succession coverage weakens; projected critical-skills gaps grow against future demand.

body.Emerging Risk: Labor-balancing policy intervention in automation and AI adoption
body.SET Risk Owner: Legal; HR; Government Affairs; Strategy
body.Risk Statement: Governments may seek to shape the pace and form of AI and automation through labor rules, oversight obligations, consultation rights, tax measures, or explicit constraints.
body.Why Emerging Now: AI labor effects are becoming politically salient and may move from social debate into direct policy intervention.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could reduce automation economics, create uneven operating models across jurisdictions, and increase friction in workforce redesign and transformation planning.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Jurisdictions introduce labor, tax, oversight, or approval requirements that materially affect automation-heavy operating models.

body.Emerging Risk: Operating-model misalignment from uneven capability adaptation and scaling lag
body.SET Risk Owner: HR; Strategy; Digital; Functional Leadership; Procurement
body.Risk Statement: Parts of AZ’s operating model may become misaligned with future business expectations if organizational design, role structures, and capability build do not adapt quickly enough to support AI30, new platforms, and growth without growing.
body.Why Emerging Now: Transformation is accelerating across AI, digital, data, and new business or platform models, but capability build, redesign speed, time-to-capability, and operating-model evolution remain uneven across functions and regions, creating risk that parts of AZ become structurally misaligned with future expectations.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could leave functions structurally less effective, increase dependence on workarounds and third parties, reduce transformation returns, and slow AZ’s ability to scale strategic capabilities for new technologies, markets, and operating models.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Major functions rely on outdated role designs, fragmented capability models, or external dependency to sustain critical transformation activity; time-to-capability becomes a constraint on strategic execution.

body.Emerging Risk: Employee trust, wellbeing, and internal legitimacy pressure under technology-led change
body.SET Risk Owner: HR; Corporate Affairs; Leadership
body.Risk Statement: Employees may increasingly question AZ’s pace and approach to AI adoption, monitoring, organizational change, and employer positioning if technology-led transformation is experienced as eroding wellbeing, fairness, or trust.
body.Why Emerging Now: Workforce expectations are evolving as AI and transformation reshape work, while change intensity, monitoring sensitivity, and the social meaning of employer choices are becoming more salient in knowledge-intensive sectors.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could affect attraction, retention, internal cohesion, change adoption, and leadership flexibility on contested issues relevant to AZ’s future operating model.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Talent attraction, retention, internal cohesion, or workforce acceptance of change is materially affected by perceived unfairness, loss of trust, or wellbeing strain linked to technology-led transformation.

body.Emerging Risk: AI-accelerated relevance decay of medicines and pipeline assets
body.SET Risk Owner: R&D; Strategy; Data and AI; Portfolio Governance
body.Risk Statement: AZ medicines and pipeline assets may lose strategic and commercial relevance faster than expected if AI transforms the speed at which competitors design, develop, and bring superior or adjacent molecules to market, or if regulators become comfortable with more AI-enabled evidence pathways.
body.Why Emerging Now: The key shift is not only more competitors, but faster compression of the value window for innovation as AI shortens cycle times, changes evidentiary expectations, and alters what counts as fast enough in science and development.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could shorten the effective strategic life of assets before exclusivity ends, bring forward revenue decline, increase late-stage portfolio attrition, and reduce the value of AZ’s historically strong R&D hit-rate and portfolio discipline.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Competitors materially accelerate target-to-IND or target-to-proof timelines in areas relevant to AZ; regulators begin accepting more AI-enabled, virtual, or in silico evidence in ways that favor faster players.
body.ER_Cluster: Rapid advances in science and competition

body.Emerging Risk: Therapy-area crowding from convergence, genericization, and adjacency migration
body.SET Risk Owner: Strategy; Commercial; Market Access; BD; Finance
body.Risk Statement: Competitors may redeploy capital and capabilities into adjacent therapeutic spaces as classes mature, patents erode, and scientific or commercial boundaries converge.
body.Why Emerging Now: High-value therapy areas attract migration where platforms, channels, biomarkers, or patient populations overlap and barriers are weakening.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could erode therapy-area leadership, intensify pricing and BD pressure, and reduce the durability of competitive advantage in priority areas.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Competitor repositioning materially increases crowding, pricing pressure, or pipeline competition in adjacent or overlapping therapy areas.
body.ER_Cluster: Rapid advances in science and competition

body.Emerging Risk: Autonomous experimentation and closed-loop science reshaping R&D advantage
body.SET Risk Owner: R&D; Strategy; Digital; IT
body.Risk Statement: Robotics, AI, active learning, automation, and increasingly autonomous experimentation may materially alter what differentiates winners in discovery and early development.
body.Why Emerging Now: Self-driving lab concepts, integrated experimentation, robotics-enabled workflows, and automated hypothesis loops are becoming more practical and strategically relevant.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could shift the economics and speed of R&D, widening the gap between organizations that can integrate autonomous science effectively and those that cannot.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Peers or challengers show meaningful cycle-time, cost, or hit-rate advantages from integrated autonomous science platforms.
body.ER_Cluster: Rapid advances in science and competition

body.Emerging Risk: Programmable biology, synthetic biology, and shared technology stacks lowering barriers to therapeutic competition
body.SET Risk Owner: Strategy; R&D; Commercial; BD
body.Risk Statement: Programmable biology, AI-enabled design, robotics, modular biomanufacturing, and reusable technical stacks may make some therapeutic areas more contestable and less protected by historical scale advantages.
body.Why Emerging Now: Convergence across synthetic biology, computation, robotics, automation, and externalized infrastructure may reduce friction for credible challengers and even local or state-backed non-traditional producers.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could shorten competitive moats, increase challenger entry, weaken biologics exclusivity assumptions in some markets, and reduce the protection historically provided by infrastructure, complexity, or specialist know-how.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: New entrants demonstrate credible entry into areas previously protected by scale, complexity, or specialist know-how; local manufacturing or abbreviated evidence acceptance weakens incumbency advantage.
body.ER_Cluster: Rapid advances in science and competition

body.Emerging Risk: Competitive advantage from proprietary data-network effects and learning speed
body.SET Risk Owner: R&D; Data and AI; Strategy; BD
body.Risk Statement: AZ may be disadvantaged if it cannot generate, integrate, learn from, protect, and operationalize unique proprietary datasets fast enough relative to platform-native competitors, or if access to strategically valuable external data becomes more costly, concentrated, or commercially restricted.
body.Why Emerging Now: Competitive differentiation is increasingly tied not just to AI access or data possession, but to closed-loop learning speed, integration quality, translational use of proprietary data, and the cost or exclusivity of accessing high-value external datasets. Durable competitive advantage may increasingly sit in trusted, differentiated data assets rather than AI alone.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could weaken R&D competitiveness, reduce differentiation, increase dependence on external data partnerships, raise the cost of capability build, and erode what may become one of AZ’s most defensible future moats.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: AZ falls behind peers or challengers in converting proprietary data into repeatable scientific, development, or commercial advantage.
body.ER_Cluster: Rapid advances in science and competition

body.Emerging Risk: Cross-TA and alliance operating-model complexity in development
body.SET Risk Owner: R&D; Strategy; Business Development; Portfolio Governance
body.Risk Statement: Increasing cross-therapeutic-area collaboration, alliance intensity, and shared-asset development may strain AZ’s historical operating model and decision pathways.
body.Why Emerging Now: AZ is pursuing more assets, platforms, and development choices that cut across legacy TA boundaries and external partnership models, increasing coordination complexity.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could slow execution, create decision friction, increase delivery risk on strategically important assets, and reduce expected returns from collaboration-intensive programs.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Important assets or programs depend on sustained cross-TA or alliance execution that proves more difficult than existing operating models support.
body.ER_Cluster: Rapid advances in science and competition

body.Emerging Risk: Platform mechanism disruption renders adjacent portfolios less relevant
body.SET Risk Owner: Strategy; R&D; Commercial; Market Access; Finance
body.Risk Statement: A broad mechanism class such as next-generation incretins may demonstrate efficacy across multiple adjacent indications and make parts of AZ’s existing or planned portfolios less relevant.
body.Why Emerging Now: The emerging issue is not the existence of GLP-1s alone, but the possibility that one platform mechanism expands across cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, metabolic, or other adjacent spaces and changes payer, prescriber, and capital-allocation behavior.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could accelerate revenue decline across affected portfolios, drive NPV write-downs, and force rapid reallocation of R&D and BD capital.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: A competitor platform mechanism achieves convincing outcomes across multiple indication areas relevant to AZ assets; payers begin consolidating around the mechanism class.
body.ER_Cluster: Rapid advances in science and competition

body.Emerging Risk: Quantum-bio-AI convergence changing capability and competition economics
body.SET Risk Owner: Strategy; R&D; IT
body.Risk Statement: Quantum, AI, automation, and programmable biology could converge to alter the economics of design, simulation, optimization, and therapeutic development.
body.Why Emerging Now: Multiple frontier technologies may reinforce one another over time and create step changes in discovery or development capability, even if some components mature more slowly than expected.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could accelerate innovation cycles, alter competitive economics, and create sharp capability gaps between leaders and laggards.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Breakthroughs begin to show scalable advantage in pharma-relevant optimization, simulation, or design tasks.
body.ER_Cluster: Rapid advances in science and competition

body.Emerging Risk: Three-bloc fracture across the US, EU, and China
body.SET Risk Owner: Strategy; Legal; Government Affairs; R&D; IT; Finance
body.Risk Statement: AZ may no longer be able to preserve one globally integrated operating model if fracture across the US, EU, and China makes simultaneous compliance, cross-border data use, technology access, scientific collaboration, and balanced participation infeasible.
body.Why Emerging Now: The risk is not just more geopolitical tension, but the possibility that the three most important blocs for AZ increasingly expect incompatible forms of participation, compliance, hosting, sourcing, and scientific alignment, forcing more regional models for trials, manufacturing, data, and even product strategy.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could force duplication of systems, infrastructure, data environments, capability, and product approaches; reduce strategic freedom; and create material sacrifice whichever side AZ prioritizes.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Legislation or enforcement makes simultaneous compliance or integrated operations materially impossible across two or more key blocs; pharma-relevant sanctions, technology restrictions, or localization demands intensify.

body.Emerging Risk: Conflict of laws and regionally conflicting compliance obligations
body.SET Risk Owner: Legal; Compliance; Government Affairs; Strategy
body.Risk Statement: AZ may face situations where overlapping legal regimes create incompatible obligations across data, trade, privacy, cyber, resilience, AI, subsidies, industrial policy, and product or infrastructure obligations.
body.Why Emerging Now: Major jurisdictions are increasingly using legislation to protect domestic capability, strategic sectors, or local rights in ways that may not align with each other, and fragmentation is spreading beyond the US, EU, and China into more actively enforcing non-core markets.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could force difficult strategic choices, increase compliance cost, constrain operating flexibility, and complicate footprint, product, reporting, and partnership decisions.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: AZ cannot readily comply with multiple applicable legal regimes simultaneously in a material business area.

body.Emerging Risk: China-centered capability acceleration and strategic competition in biopharma
body.SET Risk Owner: Strategy; R&D; BD; Commercial; Government Affairs
body.Risk Statement: China’s industrial strategy, innovation capability, manufacturing scale, and therapeutic focus may accelerate competition, alter partnering dynamics, and reshape global market assumptions relevant to AZ.
body.Why Emerging Now: China continues to invest in biotech, advanced manufacturing, health innovation, and strategic self-reliance while increasing global commercialization and licensing presence, even as foreign access to parts of the Chinese science ecosystem may become more constrained.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could challenge assumptions about speed, cost, capability leadership, partnership dynamics, and AZ’s ability to sustain advantages linked to access to Chinese science, innovation, or manufacturing ecosystems.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Chinese ecosystems materially increase speed, quality, cost competitiveness, or market influence in areas relevant to AZ; access to Chinese science or collaboration becomes more conditional.

body.Emerging Risk: Industrial policy, strategic screening, and state influence over life sciences capability
body.SET Risk Owner: Strategy; Finance; Government Affairs; Legal; Manufacturing
body.Risk Statement: Governments may increasingly shape ownership, location, access, incentives, and behavior of life sciences activity through subsidies, procurement preferences, strategic screening, localization, and regulatory leverage.
body.Why Emerging Now: Life sciences are increasingly viewed as strategically important to resilience, health security, and economic policy, with some trends resembling the treatment of other strategic sectors.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could reshape footprint decisions, distort economics, constrain transactions or collaborations, and increase regional redundancy in AZ’s operating model.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Industrial policy or state intervention materially changes capital allocation, sourcing economics, transaction feasibility, or location choices.

body.Emerging Risk: Fragmentation of global health, patient, and scientific data regimes
body.SET Risk Owner: Clinical; IT; Legal; R&D; Regulatory
body.Risk Statement: Diverging rules on genomic, clinical, patient, real-world, and sensitive health data may hinder multi-country studies, model development, evidence generation, and integrated analytics for AZ.
body.Why Emerging Now: National and regional control over health and scientific data is increasing alongside privacy, sovereignty, and strategic-data concerns, including more controlled or federated models beyond the major blocs.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could force duplicated infrastructure, reduce study efficiency, constrain evidence reuse, slow approvals, and weaken AZ’s ability to generate integrated global evidence or operate common data models.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Cross-border data use becomes materially harder in key markets, requiring separate infrastructure, revised study designs, or locally ring-fenced analytics.

body.Emerging Risk: Strategic restriction of critical materials and pharma-relevant trade dependencies
body.SET Risk Owner: Procurement; Supply Chain; Government Affairs; Strategy; Manufacturing
body.Risk Statement: States may increasingly use access to critical starting materials, specialty inputs, energy, logistics routes, or technology dependencies relevant to pharma supply and development as a source of strategic leverage, particularly as trade realigns across competing blocs.
body.Why Emerging Now: Supply restriction is becoming more plausible as geopolitical rivalry extends beyond chips and rare earths into strategic industrial and healthcare dependencies, while trade and sourcing patterns realign across competing blocs.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could disrupt AZ supply chains, raise cost, reduce resilience of health systems, force redesign of sourcing and inventory assumptions in critical categories, and reduce predictability of compliant cross-bloc trade.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Geopolitical actions materially constrain access to critical starting materials, isotopes, intermediates, or technology-dependent inputs relevant to AZ.

body.Emerging Risk: Persistent multipolar fragmentation reshaping AZ’s global operating model
body.SET Risk Owner: Strategy; Finance; Risk; Operations
body.Risk Statement: Global models based on relatively fluid movement of products, data, capital, talent, and science may become structurally less viable for AZ over the long term.
body.Why Emerging Now: Regional divergence may persist rather than normalize, making duplication and regional operating logic an enduring feature of the environment.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could permanently reduce the benefits of global scale, require regional duplication, and increase structural complexity across the enterprise.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Regional fragmentation becomes the enduring baseline for participation, manufacturing, data, and innovation strategy.

body.Emerging Risk: Fiscal and demographic erosion of the funding base for innovative medicines
body.SET Risk Owner: Market Access; Finance; Government Affairs; Strategy
body.Risk Statement: Ageing populations, below-replacement fertility, high government debt, defence spending pressure, weaker tax bases, and widening affordability politics may reduce health systems’ long-run willingness or ability to fund innovative medicines on current assumptions.
body.Why Emerging Now: This is broader than ordinary payer pressure: the concern is that structural fiscal stress changes what governments and insurers can sustainably reimburse, especially for premium therapies, while pricing becomes a wider legitimacy issue.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could compress net prices, constrain addressable populations, weaken premium pricing assumptions, and reduce expected value from innovation across multiple markets.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Governments implement fiscal measures that explicitly target innovative medicines; reimbursement becomes more restrictive on structural rather than temporary budget grounds.

body.Emerging Risk: Channel concentration, payer control, and loss of influence over therapy pathways
body.SET Risk Owner: Market Access; Commercial; Strategy; Finance
body.Risk Statement: AZ may lose influence over how therapies reach patients if payers, PBMs, integrated channels, specialty pharmacies, providers, or public-system AI intermediaries exert greater control over access, diagnosis-support, and pathway design.
body.Why Emerging Now: Healthcare systems and channels are becoming more concentrated and more able to steer distribution, reimbursement, and care pathways, while AI-based decision layers may shift influence away from manufacturers and toward payer- or provider-controlled systems.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could shift margin capture, reduce product-level influence, constrain access based on channel participation or system-owned decision tools, and weaken AZ’s ability to shape value realization.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Intermediaries materially shape access, distribution, reimbursement, diagnosis-support, or patient pathway design in ways that reduce AZ’s strategic flexibility.

body.Emerging Risk: State intervention in pricing, patent protection, and access frameworks
body.SET Risk Owner: Legal; Market Access; Government Affairs; Finance
body.Risk Statement: Fiscal stress, pricing transparency, and political pressure may increase willingness to use compulsory licensing, parallel importation, weaker patent defense, joint procurement, MFN-style architectures, or interventionist access rules to reduce medicine costs.
body.Why Emerging Now: Governments may become more willing to treat IP, pricing architecture, and access design as policy levers in response to debt, demographics, and cost pressure.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could shorten effective exclusivity, weaken pricing architecture, reduce expected returns, and increase uncertainty around launch and lifecycle value realization.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: A major market uses or credibly threatens compulsory licensing, targeted patent weakening, joint procurement, MFN expansion, or interventionist access legislation affecting innovative medicines.

body.Emerging Risk: Fragmented and more demanding evidence expectations for access and external legitimacy
body.SET Risk Owner: Regulatory; HEOR; Clinical; Market Access; Medical
body.Risk Statement: Regulators, HTA bodies, payers, and policymakers may require stronger but less harmonized evidence on real-world performance, long-term outcomes, representative populations, virtual or AI-enabled evidence, and algorithmic tools.
body.Why Emerging Now: The environment is shifting toward lifecycle evidence, post-market evaluation, and stronger scrutiny of representativeness, bias, provenance, external validity, and AI-supported evidence-generation methods.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could raise evidence-generation cost, reduce evidence reuse across markets, slow access, and create legitimacy challenges where evidence is judged insufficiently inclusive, robust, or appropriately governed.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Acceptance criteria diverge materially across markets, increasing time and cost to support access, label expansion, or policy objectives.

body.Emerging Risk: Political backlash to personalized and precision medicine
body.SET Risk Owner: Corporate Affairs; Market Access; Medical; Government Affairs; Strategy
body.Risk Statement: As AZ pioneers more personalized and precision therapies, uneven early access and high cost may create a public narrative of a two-tier system that prompts political intervention.
body.Why Emerging Now: The risk is not only affordability but the possibility that AZ becomes a visible symbol of innovation perceived to benefit too few people in too few places.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could trigger mandated contracting models, tighter pricing intervention, weaker protection of premium value, reputational spillover, and broader challenge to AZ’s leadership position in precision medicine.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Public or political narratives around unfair access to high-cost personalized medicines translate into explicit policy measures or multilateral pressure.

body.Emerging Risk: Misinformation and narrative attacks on therapeutic modalities and digital medicine
body.SET Risk Owner: Medical; Commercial; Corporate Affairs; Clinical
body.Risk Statement: Targeted misinformation may affect acceptance of modalities, vaccines, gene-based approaches, AI-enabled medicine, or digital monitoring relevant to AZ’s portfolio and strategy.
body.Why Emerging Now: Healthcare misinformation ecosystems remain adaptive, and high-salience therapeutic and digital topics are vulnerable to organized narrative attack.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could undermine recruitment, uptake, public trust, and policy sentiment in key areas, creating commercial and reputational pressure.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Misinformation measurably affects trial recruitment, prescribing, policy sentiment, or public trust in a modality or product area relevant to AZ.

body.Emerging Risk: AI backlash, anti-AI activism, and anti-pharma narrative convergence
body.SET Risk Owner: Corporate Affairs; HR; Digital; Medical; Strategy
body.Risk Statement: AZ may become a visible target of anti-AI, anti-pricing, or broader anti-pharma sentiment if AI is associated with job loss, environmental burden, opaque decision-making, reduced trust in science, or wider suspicion of AI-enabled industry.
body.Why Emerging Now: AZ’s visibility, growth profile, and ambition to embed AI across R&D and operations increase the chance that backlash against AI-intensive industries converges with wider anti-pharma and affordability narratives.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could affect reputation, recruitment, policy sentiment, freedom to deploy AI at scale, and trust in AZ’s science and operations.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: A major backlash against enterprise AI use, pharma pricing, or both leads to protests, restrictive policy, workforce activism, or targeted campaigns affecting AZ or close peers.

body.Emerging Risk: Environmental footprint, lifecycle, and product-design accountability expansion
body.SET Risk Owner: Sustainability; Legal; Corporate Affairs; Operations; Procurement; R&D
body.Risk Statement: AZ may face broader accountability for environmental externalities spanning site footprint, wastewater, residues, packaging, plastics, circularity, product lifecycle, propellants, and persistence-related concerns.
body.Why Emerging Now: Environmental scrutiny is broadening from enterprise-level sustainability commitments toward product-level, lifecycle, and sector-specific impact expectations, including product sustainability and pharmaceuticals-in-the-environment concerns.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could increase regulatory and stakeholder pressure, require redesign of products or practices, constrain operations or sourcing, and affect legitimacy in key markets.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Regulatory action, NGO pressure, procurement expectations, or disclosure requirements materially affect product, packaging, sourcing, or site decisions.
body.ER_Cluster: Sustainability, resilience and pressures on health systems

body.Emerging Risk: Critical raw material, specialty input, and supply-market volatility exposure
body.SET Risk Owner: Procurement; Supply Chain; Manufacturing; R&D; Sustainability
body.Risk Statement: AZ’s complex products and manufacturing systems may become more exposed to constrained or volatile markets for niche raw materials, components, disposables, resins, filters, assay inputs, isotopes, technology-enabling inputs, and distributor or local-market fragility.
body.Why Emerging Now: Advanced modalities, radioconjugates, geopolitical tensions, industrial transition, concentrated supply markets, and tariff or sanction effects are increasing stress on specialized input categories.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could raise cost, delay programs, constrain supply continuity, weaken commercial viability in selected modalities, and increase exposure to geopolitical and sustainability-linked disruption in key inputs and routes to market.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: A strategic input, route, or distribution dependency becomes constrained by geopolitics, concentration, sustainability requirements, or demand shifts in ways that affect continuity, programme timelines, or cost materially.
body.ER_Cluster: Sustainability, resilience and pressures on health systems

body.Emerging Risk: Site and network resilience pressure from utility, water, and local resource constraints
body.SET Risk Owner: Manufacturing; Engineering; Sustainability; Site Leadership; Strategy
body.Risk Statement: AZ’s future site and network resilience may be challenged where high-purity water dependence, utility reliability, wastewater limits, and local resource stress undermine continuity or long-term viability.
body.Why Emerging Now: Climate stress, industrial competition for resources, tightening environmental controls, and higher water stewardship expectations are making some locations more operationally constrained over time.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could create local production limits, increase resilience capex, change footprint economics, and complicate the long-term viability of selected sites or regions.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: A site or region faces recurrent water restrictions, utility stress, tighter permitting, or resource-related public pressure affecting continuity or investment assumptions.
body.ER_Cluster: Sustainability, resilience and pressures on health systems

body.Emerging Risk: Climate and nature-system shifts altering disease burden, trials, and healthcare demand
body.SET Risk Owner: Clinical; R&D; Sustainability; Strategy; Market Access
body.Risk Statement: Climate and nature-system change may alter disease patterns, trial feasibility, healthcare demand, and regional public-health priorities in ways that affect AZ’s portfolio and growth assumptions.
body.Why Emerging Now: Ecological disruption, heat stress, vector movement, health-system strain, biodiversity loss, and changing environmental exposures are increasingly influencing disease burden, trial conditions, and care demand.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could change demand patterns, trial geography, portfolio assumptions, and regional growth outlooks, requiring strategy adaptation.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Disease ecology, climate migration, environmental degradation, or health-system stress materially affects trial access, disease burden, or regional demand assumptions relevant to AZ.
body.ER_Cluster: Sustainability, resilience and pressures on health systems

body.Emerging Risk: Sustainability standards volatility and transition-cost escalation
body.SET Risk Owner: Sustainability; Finance; Operations; Corporate Affairs; Strategy
body.Risk Statement: AZ may face rising cost, target-reset pressure, assurance burden, and credibility risk if sustainability standards, reporting expectations, and transition requirements change faster than current plans, technologies, governance, or market mechanisms can absorb.
body.Why Emerging Now: External standards and stakeholder expectations are evolving across emissions, nature, value-chain accountability, and acceptable transition mechanisms, while growth and new facilities may increase the difficulty and cost of delivery and require finance-grade ESG data and assurance.
body.Potential Enterprise Impact: Could increase compliance, reporting, assurance, and transition cost, weaken confidence in targets, affect access to sustainability-linked financing or stakeholder support, require redesign of decarbonization pathways, and create reputational pressure if AZ is seen as lagging peers or relying on less accepted approaches.
body.Key Active Risk Triggers: Material external standard changes, target methodology changes, or accepted-abatement assumptions shift in ways that increase cost or reduce the viability of current plans.
